tagline: A spine everyone walks through, then four branching tracks — sized to sustain years of content, not months.
accessibility_bar: A reader with zero coding background must finish a lesson having genuinely understood it, not skimmed it. Benchmark: Ruben Hassid's writing and CS50's reputation for rigor without losing beginners.
structure_note: Modeled on how real large curricula are actually shaped (CS50, The Odin Project, freeCodeCamp, roadmap.sh, teachyourselfcs.com): one linear foundational spine, then parallel branching tracks so depth can keep growing indefinitely in any direction instead of being capped by a single list.

spine.name: The Spine
spine.who_its_for: Everyone starts here, in order. Zero assumed knowledge.
spine.source_inspiration: CS50 (Scratch/C/Python weeks) + The Odin Project's Foundations path

topics.topic: What code actually is / how a program runs
topics.plain_english_summary: A program is just instructions the computer follows in order, top to bottom.

project.title: Email Signature Generator
project.description: A 4-line script that prints a ready-to-use professional email signature. Predict each line before running it, then actually copy it into your real email client.

quiz.question: What will this print? print("Good morning")
quiz.explanation: print shows whatever is inside the quotes, exactly as written. The quotes themselves don't appear.
quiz.hint: Look only at what's between the quotes.

quiz.question: Which one will actually work and show Hello on the screen?
quiz.explanation: Text needs quotes around it so Python knows it's text, and the instruction is print. Without quotes, Python looks for something named Hello and fails.
quiz.hint: Two things matter: quotes around text, and the exact instruction name.

quiz.question: If you swapped lines 1 and 2 of the signature program, what would show first?
quiz.hint: The computer always starts at the top line.
quiz.explanation: Python runs lines top to bottom, so whichever line is first runs first. After the swap, the job title line is first.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short Python script that prints a ready-to-use email signature with my name, job title, contact details, and LinkedIn link, one print() line per piece of information. Keep it beginner friendly, with a comment explaining what print() actually does on each line.

topics.plain_english_summary: The text-only way to talk directly to your computer, no clicking — every real developer tool assumes you can use one.

project.title: Navigate & Organize Your Own Project Folders
project.description: Use cd, ls, mkdir and mv to tidy a messy folder, in a safe practice terminal.

quiz.question: After running mv file.txt NewFolder, which folder is file.txt inside now?
quiz.explanation: mv moves the thing you name first into the folder you name second, so file.txt now sits inside NewFolder.
quiz.hint: mv moves the first thing you name into the second.

quiz.question: What happens if you type a command the terminal doesn't recognise, like lss instead of ls?
quiz.explanation: The terminal only runs commands it knows. A typo gives an error such as 'command not found'; it never guesses what you meant.
options: It shows an error such as 'command not found'
It fixes the typo for you
quiz.hint: Does the terminal ever guess what you meant?

quiz.question: You're in your home folder, and file.txt is inside Week1. Which command moves it into Week1/NewFolder without using cd first?
quiz.hint: mv looks in your current folder unless you give it the route to the file.
quiz.explanation: Giving the full route from where you're standing works from anywhere: Week1/file.txt is the file, Week1/NewFolder is the destination.

topics.ai_prompt: Write me the exact terminal commands (cd, ls, mkdir, mv) to go into a folder called Week1, see what's inside, create a folder called NewFolder, and move file.txt into it. Explain what each command does, and why mv fails with 'No such file or directory' if I run it from the wrong folder.

topics.plain_english_summary: A labeled box that holds a value so you can reuse it later.

project.title: Digital Business Card Generator
project.description: Store name, title, company in variables, print a formatted card.

quiz.question: After running name = "Nabilah Azman", what does print(name) show?
quiz.explanation: print(name) opens the box labelled name and shows what's inside. The quotes aren't part of the value, so they don't appear.
quiz.hint: What did the line name = ... put in the box?

quiz.question: What happens if you run print(phone) but never stored anything in phone?
quiz.explanation: Python runs top to bottom, and no line ever created phone, so it stops with NameError: name 'phone' is not defined.
quiz.hint: Python runs top to bottom. Was phone ever stored?

quiz.question: After name = "Aisyah", what does print("Hi", name) show?
quiz.hint: The comma puts a space between the two things print shows.
quiz.explanation: print shows the text Hi, then whatever is in the name box, with a space between them because of the comma.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short Python script that stores my name, job title, and company in variables, then prints a simple digital business card using those variables. Add a comment explaining what error happens if you try to print a variable before it has been assigned a value.

topics.plain_english_summary: Math and comparisons — the same symbols as a calculator, plus knowing text from numbers from true/false.

project.title: Freelance Day-Rate Calculator
project.description: Hours × rate, apply a simple deduction.

quiz.question: In the day-rate calculator, total_cost is 400. What is the result of total_cost * 0.1?
quiz.explanation: 10% of 400 is 40. Because 0.1 is a float, the answer is a float too, so Python shows 40.0.
quiz.hint: 10% of 400. And 0.1 is a float, so the answer is a float too.

quiz.question: What happens when you run 50 + "8"?
quiz.explanation: "8" in quotes is text, not a number. Python won't add a number to text, so it stops with a TypeError instead of guessing.
quiz.hint: "8" in quotes is text. Can Python add a number and text?

quiz.question: With hourly_rate = 60 and hours_worked = 5, what is final_cost?
quiz.hint: Work it step by step: total, then 10% deduction, then subtract.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short Python script that calculates a freelance day rate: multiply hours worked by an hourly rate, then take off a 10 percent deduction, and print the final amount. Use plain variables and basic math operators. Add a comment explaining why the answer shows .0 at the end, and what error happens if a number is accidentally stored as text, like "8".

topics.plain_english_summary: How code stores and combines words and sentences.

project.title: LinkedIn Post Character Counter
project.description: Character count, word count and an over the limit check for LinkedIn's 3,000 character limit.

quiz.question: What is the result of len("Hi there")?
quiz.explanation: len counts every character, and the space counts too: H, i, space, t, h, e, r, e makes 8.
quiz.hint: Count every character, and the space counts too.

quiz.question: What does "Hello" == "hello" give?
quiz.explanation: == checks for an exact match, character by character. A capital H and a small h are different characters, so the answer is False.
quiz.hint: == checks for an exact match, character by character.

quiz.question: How many words does "Saved 8 hours".split() give?
quiz.hint: Count the pieces between the spaces.
quiz.explanation: split cuts the text at every space, giving Saved, 8 and hours: 3 pieces. The 8 counts as a word too.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short beginner Python script, without functions or if statements, that stores a LinkedIn post draft in a variable, then prints its character count with len(), its word count with split(), and True or False for whether it's over LinkedIn's 3,000 character limit, using f-strings. Add a comment explaining why "Hello" and "hello" count as different strings.

topics.plain_english_summary: An ordered row of items the code can loop through.

project.title: Weekly Task Tracker
project.description: Read, add and remove tasks stored in a list.

quiz.question: With tasks = ["Buy milk", "Walk the dog", "Do homework"], what does tasks[1] give?
quiz.explanation: Positions start at 0, so tasks[0] is Buy milk and tasks[1] is the second item, Walk the dog.
quiz.hint: Positions start at 0, so position 1 is the second item.

quiz.question: What happens if you ask for tasks[3] when the list has only three items?
quiz.explanation: Three items sit at positions 0, 1 and 2. There's no position 3, so Python stops with IndexError: list index out of range.
quiz.hint: Three items sit at positions 0, 1 and 2.

quiz.question: A list has 3 tasks. After tasks.append("Pay rent"), what does len(tasks) give?
quiz.hint: append adds exactly one item.
quiz.explanation: append adds one item to the end, so the list goes from 3 items to 4.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short Python script for a to-do list using a Python list: read the first task by its index, add a task with append, remove the last task with pop, and print the list after each step. Add a comment explaining why positions start at 0 and what IndexError means.

topics.plain_english_summary: A list that can't change, and a list with no duplicates allowed.

project.title: Duplicate Email Remover
project.description: Clean a messy newsletter recipient list using a set.

quiz.question: What type does set(email_list) create, the one that removes duplicates?
quiz.explanation: A set holds each item only once, so turning the list into a set removes the repeated email.
quiz.hint: Which type holds each item only once?

quiz.question: What happens if you try to modify a tuple after it is created?
options: It will be converted to a list
quiz.explanation: Tuples can't be changed after they're made, so Python stops with TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment.
quiz.hint: Can a tuple be changed after it's made?

quiz.question: How many items are in set(["a", "b", "a", "c", "b"])?
quiz.hint: Cross out every repeat.
quiz.explanation: A set keeps each item once, so the repeated a and b disappear, leaving a, b and c: 3 items.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short Python script that takes a list of email addresses with some duplicates, removes the duplicates using a set, and prints how many there were before and after. Then show a tuple and what error happens if you try to change it. Add a comment explaining why the set may print the emails in a different order.

topics.plain_english_summary: A lookup table by name — the same shape as the JSON every Bell tool sends around.

project.title: Client Contact Book
project.description: Add, search, update, delete records. Reused repeatedly in later tracks.

quiz.question: What is printed when you run print(contact_book["John Doe"]) after adding contact_book["John Doe"] = "012-345-6789"?
quiz.explanation: contact_book["John Doe"] looks up the key John Doe and gives back its value, the phone number.
quiz.hint: The key goes in, its value comes out.

quiz.question: What happens when you try to access a key that does not exist in the dictionary like contact_book["Jane Doe"]?
quiz.explanation: Jane Doe was never added as a key, so the lookup stops with KeyError: 'Jane Doe'. Using .get() would give a fallback instead.
quiz.hint: Was Jane Doe ever added as a key?

quiz.question: After contact_book = {"John Doe": "012"} then contact_book["John Doe"] = "098", how many pairs does the dictionary hold?
quiz.hint: Can a dictionary hold the same key twice?
quiz.explanation: Each key appears only once. Using the same key again replaces John's number instead of adding a second John.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short Python script for a simple contact book using a dictionary, with name as the key and phone number as the value, that lets me add, search, update, and delete a contact. Add a comment explaining what error happens if I search for a name that was never added.

topics.plain_english_summary: How code makes a decision.

project.title: Mini Job Offer Scorer (no AI)
project.description: Hand written if/else scoring, a simple version of the AI powered 'Should I Take This Job?' tool.

quiz.question: With salary = 5000 and location = "KL", what does the scorer print?
quiz.explanation: 5000 > 5000 is False, so the else branch sets score to 5. Then KL adds 2, giving 7.
quiz.hint: Is 5000 greater than 5000?

quiz.question: Which line makes a salary of exactly 5000 score 10 points?
quiz.explanation: >= means more than or equal to, so 5000 >= 5000 is True. With > alone, 5000 falls into the else.
quiz.hint: > means strictly more than. Which sign includes equal?

quiz.question: With salary = 5001 and location = "Penang", what score does the scorer print?
quiz.hint: Check each if separately: the salary first, then the location.
quiz.explanation: 5001 > 5000 is True, so score is 10. location == "KL" is False, so no bonus is added.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short beginner Python script, without functions, that scores a job offer using if/else: a salary over 5000 gets 10 points, otherwise 5, and a KL location adds 2 bonus points. Then print the score. Add a comment explaining what score a salary of exactly 5000 gets, and how changing > to >= changes that.

topics.plain_english_summary: Repeating an action for every item in a list.

project.title: Batch Invoice Number Generator
project.description: Print a run of sequential invoice numbers from a starting number and a quantity. It prints numbers only; it doesn't create invoice documents.

quiz.question: What is the first value range(1001, 1006) produces?
quiz.hint: range starts at the first number you give it, not one before or after it.
quiz.explanation: range starts at its first number, so the first value is 1001.

quiz.question: How many values does range(1001, 1006) produce?
quiz.hint: List them out: 1001, 1002, ... and remember the stop, 1006, is never included.
quiz.explanation: It produces 1001, 1002, 1003, 1004 and 1005, then stops before 1006. That's 5 values.

quiz.question: With start = 2001 and count = 10, what is the last invoice number range(start, start + count) prints?
quiz.hint: Work out the stop first: start + count. Then the last number printed is one less than the stop.
quiz.explanation: The stop is 2001 + 10 = 2011, which is never printed, so the last number is 2011 - 1 = 2010.

quiz.question: With start = 3001 and count = 4, what is the last invoice number printed?
quiz.hint: Use last printed = start + count - 1.
quiz.explanation: 3001 + 4 - 1 = 3004. The loop prints 3001, 3002, 3003 and 3004: four numbers.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short Python script with two variables, start and count, that uses a for loop with range(start, start + count) to print a run of invoice numbers as 'Invoice Number: X'. Add comments explaining why range stops one before start + count, why the last number printed is start + count - 1, and that this only prints numbers rather than creating invoice files.

topics.plain_english_summary: A named, reusable block of instructions.

project.title: Turn the Day-Rate Calculator into a function
project.description: Callback to S-04 — reusable across multiple clients.

quiz.question: What does day_rate_calculator(6, 80) give back?
quiz.hint: Fill the slots: hours becomes 6 and rate becomes 80. Then work out total.
quiz.explanation: hours is 6 and rate is 80, so total = 6 * 80 = 480, and return hands back 480.

quiz.question: What happens if the line that calls a function comes above its def?
quiz.hint: Python reads top to bottom. Has it seen the def yet when it reaches the call?
quiz.explanation: Python reads top to bottom, so at that point the function doesn't exist yet and it stops with a NameError.

quiz.question: If the function ended with print(total) instead of return total, what would print(client_a) show?
quiz.hint: print only shows a value on screen. What does a function hand back when it has no return?
quiz.explanation: Without return the function hands back None, Python's word for nothing, so client_a is None. The 400 was only shown on screen, never handed back.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short Python script that turns a day rate calculation, hours times hourly rate, into a reusable function with return, then calls it for two different clients and prints both totals. Add a comment explaining what error happens if the function is called before its def line.

topics.plain_english_summary: Why searching a phone book alphabetically beats reading every name — a first taste of what Track D later formalizes as Big-O.

project.title: Compare two ways of searching the Contact Book
project.description: Count the steps for checking every entry one by one versus a dictionary lookup.

quiz.question: Searching one by one through 5 names, how many names are checked to find the last one?
quiz.explanation: A linear search checks every name in order until it finds the target. The last one is only reached after checking all 5.
quiz.hint: Think about how many names each method has to look at.

quiz.question: Why does a dictionary lookup stay fast as the contact book grows?
quiz.explanation: Python uses the key itself to work out where the value is stored, so it goes straight there instead of checking names one by one.
options: It checks every name twice as fast
It goes straight to the entry using the key
quiz.hint: Think about how many names each method has to look at.

quiz.question: In a list of 1,000 names, the one you want is the 600th. How many names does a one by one search check to find it?
quiz.hint: A one by one search starts at the first name and stops when it finds the one it wants.
quiz.explanation: It checks names 1, 2, 3 and so on, and stops at the 600th, so it checks 600 names. A dictionary lookup would go straight to it.

topics.ai_prompt: Write me a short beginner Python script that searches for a name in a list one by one, counting each step, and then looks the same name up in a dictionary by its key. Print how many steps the one by one search took. Add comments explaining why the dictionary lookup stays fast even when the list is much bigger.

topics.plain_english_summary: Borrowing pre-written code instead of writing everything from scratch.

project.title: Secure Password Generator
project.description: Uses Python's built-in random and string modules.

quiz.question: If you run print(generate_password(12)), how many characters long is the password?
quiz.explanation: The loop runs length times, adding one random character each round, so 12 rounds make 12 characters.
quiz.hint: The loop runs once per character. How many times does it run?

quiz.question: Which module should you use to pick random characters for a password?
quiz.explanation: Python's documentation says to use secrets for anything security related. The random module is designed for simulations and games, and its results can be predicted.
quiz.hint: One of these is designed for games and simulations, the other for security.

quiz.question: How many characters can secrets.choice pick from in string.ascii_letters + string.digits + string.punctuation?
quiz.hint: Count each part: 52 letters (a to z and A to Z), 10 digits, and the punctuation symbols.
quiz.explanation: 52 letters + 10 digits + 32 punctuation symbols = 94 characters to choose from.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short Python script that generates a secure random password of a length I choose, using Python's built in secrets and string modules and a simple for loop. Add a comment explaining why secrets is used instead of random, and what error happens if you forget to import a module first.

topics.plain_english_summary: Telling the program what to do instead of crashing.

project.title: Safe Cost per Unit Calculator
project.description: Divide total cost by units, and handle a units figure of 0 with try/except instead of crashing.

quiz.question: With units = 0, what does the cost per unit calculator do?
quiz.explanation: Dividing by 0 raises a ZeroDivisionError, so Python skips to the matching except and prints its message instead of stopping.
options: Prints "Can not work out cost per unit: units is 0."
quiz.hint: Does the division succeed when units is 0?

quiz.question: Why is except ZeroDivisionError: safer than a bare except:?
quiz.explanation: A bare except catches every error, so an unexpected problem gets a wrong message and goes unnoticed. Naming the error means anything else still shows up.
options: It only catches the problem you planned for, so other errors still show
It stops all errors from happening
quiz.hint: What happens to errors you didn't plan for?

quiz.question: With units = 0, which line of the program never runs?
quiz.hint: Python skips the rest of the try block as soon as one line in it fails.
quiz.explanation: The division on the line before it fails, so Python abandons the rest of the try block, including this print, and jumps to the except.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short Python script that works out cost per unit by dividing a total cost by a number of units, using try/except to catch a ZeroDivisionError when units is 0 instead of crashing. Add a comment explaining why catching only ZeroDivisionError is safer than a bare except.

topics.plain_english_summary: How code saves something to disk and reads it back.

project.title: Expense Log
project.description: Save entries to a file, read the running total back next run.

quiz.question: Which mode adds a new line to the end of a file and keeps what's already there?
quiz.explanation: "a" means append: it adds to the end. "w" empties the file first, and "r" only reads.
quiz.hint: One of these adds to the end, one empties the file first.

quiz.question: If the expense log adds Rent,1000 on every run, what running total does the second run print?
quiz.explanation: After two runs the file holds two lines of 1000. The loop adds them up, and float makes the total 2000.0.
quiz.hint: Each run adds one line. How many lines after two runs?

quiz.question: expenses.txt holds two lines: Rent,1000 and Food,50.5. What running total does the program print?
quiz.hint: Add the two amounts after the commas.
quiz.explanation: The loop adds float("1000") and float("50.5"): 1000.0 + 50.5 = 1050.5.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short Python script that appends an expense line like Rent,1000 to a text file every time it runs, then reads every line back and prints the running total. Use with open(...) and append mode. Add a comment explaining why "w" mode would wipe out the previous expenses.

topics.plain_english_summary: Getting someone else's code onto your machine, and why projects keep separate toolboxes.

project.title: Newsletter Signup QR Code Generator
project.description: pip install qrcode — first external package, immediately usable output.

quiz.question: Which command switches on the virtual environment in the .venv folder on a Mac?
quiz.explanation: python3 -m venv .venv only creates the toolbox. source .venv/bin/activate switches it on for this terminal window, and your prompt then starts with (.venv).
quiz.hint: One command creates the toolbox, another switches it on.

quiz.question: You installed qrcode, open a new terminal, run your script and get ModuleNotFoundError. What's the most likely cause?
quiz.explanation: The package lives inside the virtual environment, which isn't switched on in the new window. Activate it again and the import works.
options: The virtual environment isn't activated in this window
quiz.hint: Is the toolbox switched on in a brand new terminal window?

quiz.question: What does (.venv) at the start of your terminal line tell you?
quiz.hint: It appears right after you run source .venv/bin/activate.
quiz.explanation: It means the virtual environment is switched on in this window, so pip installs into it and python uses its packages.
options: The virtual environment is switched on in this window

topics.ai_prompt: Give me the exact terminal commands to create and activate a Python virtual environment on a Mac and install the qrcode package with image support (qrcode[pil]), plus a short Python script that turns a link into a QR code image and saves it. Add a comment explaining why the package should be installed inside a virtual environment.

topics.plain_english_summary: What actually protects your work from being lost — moved early because every real curriculum (CS50, Odin) teaches it right after basics, not as a late afterthought.

project.title: Turn Week 1_Excel Formula Generator into a real git repo
project.description: A genuinely real, unresolved gap found this session: these folders have zero backup or history.

quiz.question: Which command takes the snapshot of your staged files, with a note?
quiz.explanation: git add only picks files for the snapshot. git commit -m takes it and attaches your note.
quiz.hint: add picks files; which command takes the snapshot?

quiz.question: You made good edits, never committed, then ran git restore on the file. What happens to the good edits?
quiz.explanation: git restore puts the file back exactly as it was in the last commit, so anything you never committed is gone.
quiz.hint: git restore goes back to the last commit. Were the edits ever committed?

quiz.question: git status --short shows ?? next to a file. What does that mean?
quiz.hint: Has the file ever been added to git?
quiz.explanation: ?? means untracked: git can see the file but it isn't in any snapshot yet. git add stages it, then it shows A.
options: Git sees the file but isn't tracking it yet

topics.ai_prompt: Write me the exact sequence of git commands to set my name and email once, turn a project folder into a git repository, check its status, stage a file, make my first commit, and view the history. Give a one sentence explanation of each command, and a note on why committing every time something works matters.

topics.plain_english_summary: Pushing your git repo somewhere safe off your laptop.

project.title: Push the Week 1 repo to GitHub
project.description: Newsletter, Bell_Assistant, sanyu-app are already-working real examples to reference.

quiz.question: Which command sends your commits up to GitHub for the first time?
quiz.explanation: push sends your commits to the online copy called origin, on the main branch. The -u remembers the pairing so later you can just type git push.
quiz.hint: push sends commits to origin, on the main branch.

quiz.question: Your laptop is lost. Which commits survive?
quiz.explanation: Commits only reach GitHub when you push. Anything committed but never pushed was only on the laptop.
quiz.hint: Commits only reach GitHub when you push.

quiz.question: git push -u origin main fails with src refspec main does not match any. Which command fixes it?
quiz.hint: The error says there's nothing called main to push.
quiz.explanation: Your branch is still called master, so there's no main to push. git branch -M main renames it, then the push works.

topics.ai_prompt: Write me the exact git commands to connect a local git repository to a new, empty GitHub repository and push it for the first time, including git branch -M main. Explain what each command does, and that GitHub needs a personal access token instead of my password when I push.

topics.plain_english_summary: The structure/skeleton of every webpage you've ever visited.

project.title: Build a one-page 'About Me' site
project.description: Pure structure first, no styling — headings, paragraphs, a list, a link.

quiz.question: Which tag makes the main heading in <h1>Hi, I'm Nabilah</h1>?
quiz.explanation: h1 stands for heading level 1, the biggest and most important heading on the page.
quiz.hint: h1 is short for heading level 1.

quiz.question: What happens if you forget the closing </a> tag?
quiz.explanation: Browsers guess where an unclosed tag ends, and often guess wrong, so the text after the link can turn into part of it.
options: Text after the link can become part of the link
The browser refuses to open the page
quiz.hint: Browsers try to guess where an unclosed tag ends.

quiz.question: Which tag sets the text shown on the browser tab?
quiz.hint: It goes inside <head>, with the information about the page.
quiz.explanation: <title> goes inside <head>, and its text appears on the browser tab, not on the page itself.

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a simple one page About Me website in plain HTML, starting with <!DOCTYPE html> and a meta charset line, with a heading, a short paragraph about me, a bullet list of my skills, and a link to my LinkedIn. Add a comment reminding me why every tag I open needs a matching closing tag.

topics.plain_english_summary: How that skeleton gets colors, spacing, and layout.

project.title: Style the About Me page in Bell brand colors
project.description: Apply navy/gold/cream to the S-19 project.

quiz.question: With body { color: #1A1A2E; }, what colour is the page text?
quiz.explanation: color sets the text colour, and #1A1A2E is The Bell's navy.
quiz.hint: color sets the text colour.

quiz.question: What does CSS control?
quiz.explanation: HTML decides what each part of the page is. CSS decides how it looks, including colours, fonts, spacing and where things sit on the page.
options: The content and words on the page
How the page looks, including colours, fonts and layout
quiz.hint: HTML is what's on the page; CSS is how it looks.

quiz.question: You write colour: #1A1A2E; (British spelling). What happens?
quiz.hint: CSS uses American spelling, and it never shows an error message.
quiz.explanation: CSS doesn't show errors. The browser doesn't know a property called colour, so it quietly skips that line and the text keeps its default colour.
options: The browser ignores that line, so the text colour doesn't change

topics.ai_prompt: Take a simple About Me HTML page and add a CSS style block in the head that uses a cream background (#F5F0E8), navy text (#1A1A2E), a gold accent (#C9A84C) as a line under the heading, and a centred column with max-width. Add a comment explaining why gold isn't used as the text colour on cream, and the difference between what HTML controls and what CSS controls.

topics.plain_english_summary: How a page responds to you clicking or typing, without reloading.

quiz.question: After you click the button, what does its label change to?
quiz.explanation: The click listener runs button.textContent = "Copied!", which changes the label straight away, with no page reload.
quiz.hint: Look at the line that changes the button's label.

quiz.question: Why should the <script> go after the button in the HTML?
quiz.explanation: The browser reads top to bottom. If the script runs first, the button doesn't exist yet and getElementById finds nothing.
options: Scripts at the top run slower
So the button exists when the script looks for it
quiz.hint: The browser reads the page top to bottom.

quiz.question: Which line connects the button to the code that runs when it's clicked?
quiz.hint: Look for the word click.
quiz.explanation: addEventListener("click", ...) tells the browser: when this button is clicked, run the function inside.

topics.ai_prompt: Add a real, working copy to clipboard button to my HTML page using plain JavaScript, with getElementById, addEventListener and navigator.clipboard.writeText, so clicking it copies my email address and changes the button label to Copied! without reloading the page. Add a comment explaining why the script tag goes after the button.

quiz.question: Which line in .gitignore stops git from uploading your secrets file?
quiz.explanation: Anything listed in .gitignore is skipped by git add, so a line saying .env keeps that file off GitHub.
quiz.hint: Anything listed in .gitignore is skipped by git add.

quiz.question: Your API key was pushed to a public GitHub repo, then you deleted it from the code. What should you do?
quiz.explanation: git keeps the history, so the old key is still visible. Treat it as leaked: create a new key and delete the old one.
options: Make the repo private and carry on
Create a new key and delete the old one
quiz.hint: git keeps the history of every commit.

quiz.question: .env is listed in .gitignore. After git add ., what does git status --short show for .env?
quiz.hint: Ignored files don't appear in git status.
quiz.explanation: Nothing at all: git pretends ignored files aren't there, so .env is never staged, committed or pushed.

topics.ai_prompt: Show me how to keep an API key secret in a Python project: install python-dotenv, create a .env file, add .env to .gitignore, and load the key with load_dotenv and os.getenv. quiz.question: What does client2.display_info() print?
quiz.explanation: display_info reads the attributes of the object it's called on through self, so client2 shows only Jane's details.
options: Name: John Doe, Phone: 1234567890, Address: 123 Main St
Name: Jane Tan, Phone: 0198765432, Address: 8 Jalan Ampang
quiz.hint: display_info reads the attributes of the object it's called on.

quiz.question: What does self mean inside a method?
quiz.explanation: self is the particular object the method is working on, so client1.display_info() reads client1's data and nobody else's.
options: The particular object the method is working on
quiz.hint: self is the object the method was called on.

quiz.question: When you run client2.display_info(), what does self mean inside the method?
quiz.hint: Look at what comes before the dot.
quiz.explanation: self is always the object the method was called on. client2.display_info() means self is client2, so it reads Jane's details.

quiz.question: What is the result of [x * 2 for x in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]]?
quiz.explanation: The comprehension takes each number, doubles it, and collects the results in a new list.
quiz.hint: Double each number.

quiz.question: After running doubled_numbers = [x * 2 for x in numbers], what has happened to numbers?
quiz.explanation: A comprehension always builds a brand new list. The original list is never touched.
quiz.hint: A comprehension always builds a new list.

quiz.question: What does [x + 10 for x in [1, 2, 3]] give?
quiz.hint: Do the step for each item in turn.
quiz.explanation: The comprehension takes each x, adds 10, and collects the results: 1 + 10, 2 + 10, 3 + 10.

quiz.question: What does bool(re.fullmatch(pattern, "nabilah@example")) give with the email pattern?
quiz.explanation: The pattern needs a dot and at least 2 letters after the domain, like .com. "nabilah@example" has no ending, so it doesn't fit.
quiz.hint: The pattern needs a dot and at least 2 letters after the domain.

quiz.question: An email passes the pattern check. What does that prove?
quiz.explanation: A pattern only checks the shape of the text. Whether the mailbox exists is only proven by sending to it.
options: It has the right shape for an email
quiz.hint: A pattern only checks the shape of text.

quiz.question: datetime.strptime("30/09/2026", "%Y-%m-%d"): what happens?
quiz.hint: Does the text match the layout %Y-%m-%d?
quiz.explanation: The layout says year-month-day with dashes, but the text is day/month/year with slashes, so Python stops with a ValueError: does not match format.
options: ValueError: the text doesn't match the format

topics.ai_prompt: Build me a short Python script that checks whether an invoice due date is in the past using datetime, and whether an email address has a valid format using re.fullmatch with a simple email pattern.
